lesson.title: Two Points, One Straight Line: Linear Molecules
lesson.summary: Linear geometry is the simplest possible molecular shape, placing two electron domains exactly 180 degrees apart, and it explains why carbon dioxide, despite having polar bonds, has no overall dipole.
lesson.body:
Linear geometry is what happens when a central atom has the smallest possible steric number that still allows for a shape: two electron domains and nothing else. With only two regions of electron density to keep apart, there is exactly one arrangement that maximizes the distance between them, placing the two domains on directly opposite sides of the central atom, forming a straight line with a bond angle of 180 degrees. Because this shape has no lone pairs to worry about, the electron geometry and the molecular geometry are the same thing, both are simply called linear.

Carbon dioxide, CO2, is the standard example. Carbon sits at the center, double bonded to an oxygen atom on each side. In VSEPR counting, a double bond still counts as only one electron domain, since all the bonding electrons between the same two atoms occupy the same general region of space regardless of how many pairs are shared. Carbon has two domains total, one to each oxygen, and no lone pairs, giving a steric number of two and a linear molecular geometry with a bond angle of exactly 180 degrees. This is also why carbon dioxide is nonpolar overall even though each individual C to O bond is quite polar: the two bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions along that straight line and cancel each other perfectly.

Another instructive example is hydrogen cyanide, HCN. The central carbon atom is singly bonded to hydrogen on one side and triple bonded to nitrogen on the other. Just as with the double bonds in carbon dioxide, the triple bond still counts as a single electron domain in VSEPR analysis. Carbon again has only two domains, giving a linear shape with the hydrogen, carbon, and nitrogen atoms all falling on one straight line, 180 degrees apart.

Beryllium chloride, BeCl2, offers a slightly different but equally important lesson. Beryllium has only two valence electrons, so when it forms two single bonds to chlorine atoms it ends up with just four electrons around it rather than a full octet. This is a well known exception to the octet rule, but VSEPR still applies perfectly well: two bonding domains, no lone pairs, and a linear shape with a 180 degree bond angle. The lesson is that linear geometry only requires a steric number of two, it does not require or depend on the central atom having a complete octet.

Acetylene, C2H2, shows that linear geometry can appear more than once within the same molecule. Each carbon atom is bonded to one hydrogen and triple bonded to the other carbon, giving each carbon exactly two electron domains and therefore a linear arrangement around it. The result is a molecule where every atom, both hydrogens and both carbons, lies along a single straight line. Linear geometry, though the simplest shape VSEPR can produce, shows up constantly across organic and inorganic chemistry wherever a central atom is left with only two regions of electron density to manage.
